questions.retired_reason: Superseded by the v2 pool (cue-free rewrite, 2026-10-22)

questions.stem: Which statement about validation tests is NOT true?

options.text: They confirm that recovery procedures work
They are discussion-only, with no systems touched
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: that is a tabletop exercise.

questions.explanation: Validation tests are hands-on tests that confirm recovery procedures and systems work. Unlike a tabletop, they actually exercise systems.
questions.discriminator_tested: Validation actually exercises systems.
questions.retired_reason: Superseded by the v2 pool (cue-free rewrite, 2026-10-22)

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT typically part of a disaster recovery plan?

options.rationale: Correct choice: unrelated to restoring IT.

questions.explanation: A disaster recovery plan holds the documented procedures for restoring IT systems and data after a disruption. It is focused on IT restoration.
questions.discriminator_tested: The DRP is focused on IT restoration.
questions.retired_reason: Superseded by the v2 pool (cue-free rewrite, 2026-10-22)

questions.stem: During a regional flood, staff work from a partner office, customer calls are rerouted, and payroll is run by hand while IT restores the servers. Which plan covers all of this?

options.rationale: The DRP covers only the IT restoration part.

options.text: The business continuity plan, which is broader than IT and includes the DRP
options.rationale: Correct: it keeps business operations going, not just IT.

questions.explanation: A business continuity plan keeps critical business operations running during and after a disruption. It is broader than IT, and the DRP is part of it.
questions.discriminator_tested: The BCP is broader than IT; the DRP is part of it.
questions.retired_reason: Superseded by the v2 pool (cue-free rewrite, 2026-10-22)

questions.stem: A company raises its data center floor and installs flood barriers. It also keeps a plan for restoring its servers at another site after a flood. What BEST describes the flood barriers' role?

options.rationale: True, but it misses the prevention-versus-recovery point.

options.text: Risk transfer to the building owner
options.rationale: Nothing is shifted to another party.
That is the role of the restoration plan.
Correct: barriers reduce the chance of the event.

questions.explanation: Disaster prevention and recovery work together: prevention lowers the likelihood of disruptive events, and recovery restores operations when they happen anyway.
questions.discriminator_tested: Prevention lowers likelihood; recovery restores service.

questions.stem: In the same week, a user deletes a project folder and ransomware encrypts a file share. What is the PRIMARY defense against both kinds of loss?

options.rationale: May stop the ransomware, but not an accidental deletion.

options.text: A UPS on the file server
options.rationale: Protects against power loss, not data loss.
Mirrors the deletion and the encryption too.
Correct: they bring back deleted and encrypted data alike.

questions.explanation: Data loss comes from hardware failure, deletion, corruption, ransomware, or disaster. Backups are the primary defense; redundancy such as RAID copies mistakes as faithfully as data.
questions.discriminator_tested: Backups are the primary defense against data loss.

questions.stem: A server's nightly backup copies its Data and Users folders and nothing else. The server's boot disk fails. What is the MOST likely result?

options.text: OS and apps must be rebuilt first
options.rationale: Correct: file-level backups can't rebuild a whole system alone.

options.text: A bare-metal restore from the backup

options.rationale: True, but it misses the rebuild.

questions.explanation: File-level backups copy selected files and folders. They are fast and small and restore individual files, but they can't rebuild a whole system on their own.
questions.discriminator_tested: File-level backups can't rebuild a whole system alone.

questions.stem: Which two can an image-based backup do that a file-level backup can't do on its own? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: it captures the entire system.
That is a network device config backup.
Correct: the whole disk, onto new hardware.

questions.explanation: Image-based backups capture the entire disk or system: OS, applications, settings, and data. They enable a full-system (bare-metal) restore, at the cost of size.
questions.discriminator_tested: Image backups enable bare-metal restore; larger.

questions.stem: A company's backup plan is shown below. What is MOST clearly missing?
questions.exhibit:
Application          Backup    Restore order
Order processing     Weekly    Any
Payroll              Weekly    Any
Intranet blog        Weekly    Any
Old project archive  Weekly    Any

options.rationale: Worth having, but it doesn't fix the priorities.
For some apps, yes, but which ones depends on criticality.
Correct: it sets backup frequency and recovery order.

questions.explanation: Critical applications are those essential to operations. Identifying them sets backup frequency and recovery order; priority comes from business criticality.
questions.discriminator_tested: Priority comes from business criticality.

questions.stem: An admin backs up a router as shown below. What is the BEST improvement?
questions.exhibit:
R1# copy running-config tftp:
Address or name of remote host []? 10.1.9.5
Destination filename [r1-confg]?
!!
2391 bytes copied in 0.412 secs

options.rationale: Correct: TFTP is unauthenticated and unencrypted.
Scheduling helps, but the transfer is still insecure.
Routers hold configs, not user data.

options.text: Save a copy to flash as well
options.rationale: A local copy is lost with the router.

questions.explanation: Network device backup and restore saves device configurations (for example, copy running-config to a remote server) and restores them after a failure. It backs up configs, not user data, and secure transfer is preferred over TFTP.
questions.discriminator_tested: Prefer secure transfer over TFTP.

questions.stem: Management says the order system must be back within 4 hours of an outage, and no more than 15 minutes of orders may be lost. Which values are these?

options.rationale: Correct: RTO is how long; RPO is how much data.
MTTR is an average repair time, not a target.

questions.explanation: Data restoration characteristics describe how fast and how current a restore is. RTO is the time to restore; RPO is the tolerable data loss, set by the age of the last backup.
questions.discriminator_tested: RTO = how long; RPO = how much data.

questions.stem: A company wants one backup copy that ransomware on its network can't reach and that survives losing the building. Which BEST fits?

options.text: A NAS in the server room

options.rationale: Offsite, but an always-connected copy can be encrypted too.

options.text: A second disk in each server

questions.explanation: Backup media include disk or NAS, tape, cloud, and removable media, each with trade-offs in cost, speed, capacity, and durability. Offline or offsite media survive ransomware and site loss.
questions.discriminator_tested: Offline or offsite media survive ransomware and site loss.

questions.stem: Using the schedule below, which backups are needed to restore the server to its Wednesday-night state?
questions.exhibit:
Backup schedule (file server)
Sun 23:00  Full
Mon 23:00  Incremental
Tue 23:00  Incremental
Wed 23:00  Incremental
Thu 08:15  Disk failure

options.rationale: Correct: each incremental holds changes since the previous backup.
That works for differentials, not incrementals.

questions.explanation: Backup methods: full copies everything, incremental copies changes since the last backup of any type, and differential copies changes since the last full. Incremental is the fastest backup but the slowest restore: the full plus every incremental.
questions.discriminator_tested: Incremental restore needs the full plus every incremental.

questions.stem: Backup jobs have reported success every night for two years. In a real outage, the restore fails because the backup files are corrupt. What BEST describes the root cause?

options.rationale: Correct: a test restore would have exposed the corruption.
The jobs reported success, so alerts wouldn't help.

questions.explanation: Backup testing means periodically restoring data to verify integrity, completeness, and timing. An untested backup is unproven, whatever the job logs say.
questions.discriminator_tested: An untested backup is unproven.

questions.stem: Attackers hijack executives' email by porting their phone numbers to new SIMs and then using SMS password reset. What BEST reduces this risk?

options.text: Alerts to users when a reset happens
options.rationale: Detects the takeover, but doesn't prevent it.

options.text: App- or key-based recovery instead of SMS
options.rationale: Correct: removes the weak recovery channel.

questions.explanation: Online account recovery resets access through email, phone, recovery codes, or MFA. The recovery channel is itself an attack path, so protect it.
questions.discriminator_tested: The recovery channel is an attack path.

questions.stem: A user forgets the password to a local account on a standalone workstation that isn't in a domain. Who can reset it?

options.rationale: Self-service resets are for directory accounts.
Correct: local recovery needs a second admin or recovery media.
The PC isn't in a domain.

questions.explanation: Local account recovery is a reset by another local administrator or with recovery media or tools. It depends on a second admin account or physical access; there is no central reset.
questions.discriminator_tested: Local recovery: second admin or physical access.

questions.stem: Which two are typical ways to recover a locked-out domain account? (Choose two.)

options.text: Signing in with another local admin account
options.rationale: Changes local accounts, not domain ones.

options.text: Booting the PC from password-recovery media

questions.explanation: Domain account recovery is a reset or unlock by a domain administrator or help desk in the directory. It is managed centrally, and self-service reset is possible.
questions.discriminator_tested: Domain recovery is central; self-service possible.

questions.stem: A small office plans to keep its network closet running through utility outages with a battery backup unit. What is the MAIN limitation?

options.rationale: True over the years, but not the main limit.

options.text: It takes minutes to start up

options.rationale: Many do; runtime is the issue.

questions.explanation: A battery backup provides short-term power during an outage. Its runtime is in minutes, not hours.
questions.discriminator_tested: Battery runtime is minutes, not hours.

questions.stem: During a 2-hour outage, a UPS-protected server runs for 12 minutes, then loses power and corrupts its database. What was MOST clearly missing?

options.text: A switched PDU in the rack
A surge protector on the circuit
A UPS with a bigger battery pack
options.rationale: Buys more minutes, but it still runs out.
Correct: a UPS bridges to one or the other.

questions.explanation: A UPS is battery-backed power that also conditions input power. It bridges to a graceful shutdown or a generator start; it isn't long-term power.
questions.discriminator_tested: UPS bridges to shutdown or generator.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a standby UPS from the other UPS types?

options.rationale: Correct: it passes utility power and switches on failure.

options.text: It corrects sags without the battery

questions.explanation: A standby UPS passes utility power through and switches to battery on failure. It has a brief switchover gap, the lowest cost, and the least protection.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standby: switchover gap; lowest cost.

questions.stem: Frequent voltage sags at a branch office keep switching its standby UPS to battery and wearing the battery out. Which UPS type BEST fixes this at moderate cost?

options.rationale: Correct: regulates sags without using the battery.
Fixes it too, at higher cost.
Still switches to battery on each sag.

questions.explanation: A line-interactive UPS regulates voltage sags and surges without using the battery, then switches to battery on an outage. It handles voltage fluctuation at mid-range cost.
questions.discriminator_tested: Line-interactive handles voltage fluctuation; mid-range.

questions.stem: A lab instrument resets if its power is interrupted for even a few milliseconds. Which UPS type is BEST?

options.rationale: Takes seconds or more to start.
Still has a short transfer on outage.

questions.explanation: An online UPS uses double conversion: equipment always runs from the inverter. There is no transfer time, giving the best protection at the highest cost.
questions.discriminator_tested: Online UPS: no transfer time.

questions.stem: Utility power fails at a data center that has a UPS and a diesel generator. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Generator starts, then UPS takes over
Generator takes over at once, no UPS
UPS runs the site until power returns
UPS bridges until the generator runs
options.rationale: Correct: the generator needs time to start.

questions.explanation: Power generators provide long-duration backup power (diesel or natural gas). They take time to start, so a UPS bridges the gap, and they need fuel and regular testing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Generator takes time to start; UPS bridges.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a surge protector from a UPS?

options.text: It diverts spikes but supplies no power
options.rationale: Correct: protection against spikes, not outages.
Often true, but not the functional difference.

options.text: It switches to battery on an outage
options.rationale: That is what a UPS does.

options.text: It conditions sags without a battery
options.rationale: That is a line-interactive UPS feature.

questions.explanation: Surge protection diverts excess voltage spikes away from equipment. It protects against spikes, not outages, and isn't a UPS.
questions.discriminator_tested: Surge protection: spikes, not outages.

questions.stem: Which two features do metered and switched PDUs add over a basic rack power strip? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: switched PDUs can power-cycle outlets.

questions.explanation: A PDU distributes power to rack equipment; metered and switched versions add monitoring and remote outlet control. It is distribution, not backup, and gains backup only when fed by a UPS.
questions.discriminator_tested: Metered adds monitoring; switched adds remote control.

questions.stem: A server room's cooling unit fails late on a Friday, and no one notices until Monday. What is the MOST likely result?

options.rationale: A humidity problem, not a cooling one.
Heat from equipment rarely triggers it.
Likely, but nobody acted on them.

questions.explanation: HVAC controls temperature, airflow, and humidity. Overheating causes failures, so cooling is a continuity control.
questions.discriminator_tested: Overheating causes failures; cooling is continuity.

questions.stem: A server room monitor shows the readings below. What is the MAIN environmental risk?
questions.exhibit:
Server room monitor   14:00
Temperature:          22 C
Relative humidity:    12 %
Dew point:            -9 C

options.text: No risk; both readings are fine
options.rationale: The humidity is far too low.
That comes from air that is too humid.
Correct: very dry air raises static risk.
22 C is within the recommended range.

questions.explanation: ASHRAE standards recommend temperature and humidity ranges for computing environments (about 18-27 C). Air that is too dry raises static discharge risk; too humid causes condensation and corrosion.
questions.discriminator_tested: Too dry = static; too humid = condensation.

questions.stem: A building needs fire suppression for its server room and for the staff kitchen next door. Which pairing is BEST?

options.text: A clean-agent system in both spaces
options.rationale: Works, but costly where water is fine.
Correct: match the system to the space.

options.text: Wet pipe sprinklers in both spaces

questions.explanation: Fire suppression extinguishes fires while limiting damage to people and equipment. Match the system to the space: water-based for general areas, clean agent for equipment rooms.
questions.discriminator_tested: Match the system to the space.

questions.stem: An older building's server room is covered by the building's wet pipe sprinklers. What is the MAIN risk to the servers?

options.text: Water damage during a real fire
options.rationale: True of any sprinkler, but leaks are the everyday risk.

options.text: Pipes freezing in a cold winter
options.rationale: Inside a heated building that is unlikely; it drives dry pipe use.
Correct: the pipes are full of water at all times.

questions.explanation: Wet pipe systems keep water in the pipes; heat opens a sprinkler head. They are the simplest and fastest, but accidental discharge or leaks can damage electronics.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wet pipe: leaks or accidental discharge.

questions.stem: An unheated loading dock, where winter temperatures drop below freezing, needs sprinklers. Which system BEST fits?

options.rationale: Also dry, but adds detection meant for equipment rooms.

options.text: Wet pipe sprinklers with heat tape
options.rationale: Patches the freezing risk instead of avoiding it.
Correct: gas in the pipes until a head opens.

questions.explanation: Dry pipe systems hold pressurized gas in the pipes; water enters after a head opens. They are used where pipes could freeze, at the cost of slower water delivery.
questions.discriminator_tested: Dry pipe: where pipes could freeze.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a preaction system from a dry pipe system?

options.text: Its heads open together on detection
Its pipes are dry until triggered
It uses a gas instead of water
Detection must fill the pipes first

questions.explanation: Preaction systems keep the pipes dry; water enters only after detection, and a head must then open. The two-step trigger lowers accidental-discharge risk, which makes them common in data centers.
questions.discriminator_tested: Preaction: detection, then a head must open.

questions.stem: An aircraft hangar with fuel hazards needs a system that soaks the whole area at once as soon as fire is detected. Which BEST fits?

options.rationale: Still waits for individual heads to open.
Correct: open heads discharge together on detection.
Opens head by head as heat reaches them.

questions.explanation: Deluge systems have open heads that discharge water from every head on detection. They deliver massive water flow for high-hazard areas.
questions.discriminator_tested: Deluge: massive flow for high-hazard areas.

questions.stem: What is the MAIN reason a data center chooses a clean-agent system over sprinklers?

options.text: It's cheaper to install and refill

options.rationale: Can be true, but not the main reason.
That is the reason for dry pipe.

questions.explanation: Clean agent systems use gaseous suppression that leaves no residue. There is no water damage, so they suit equipment rooms.
questions.discriminator_tested: Clean agent: no water damage, no residue.

questions.stem: A facilities manager wants to install a new halon system in the server room because halon is so effective. What BEST describes the problem?

options.rationale: True, but the ban is the real obstacle.

options.text: Halon needs a dry pipe network
options.rationale: Halon is a gaseous agent, not a sprinkler type.

options.text: Production is banned; it harms ozone
options.rationale: Correct: legacy systems remain, but no new halon is made.

questions.explanation: Halon is an effective gaseous agent that depletes ozone. Its production is banned (EPA), so legacy systems are all that remain.
questions.discriminator_tested: Halon production banned; legacy only.

questions.stem: Which suppression agent puts out a fire by lowering the oxygen in the room?

options.rationale: A chemical agent that mainly absorbs heat.

questions.explanation: Argon is an inert gas that displaces oxygen. It is safe for equipment and works by oxygen reduction, so occupants must leave before discharge.
questions.discriminator_tested: Argon works by oxygen reduction.

questions.stem: A vendor proposes NAF-S-III for a server room. What BEST describes it?

options.rationale: It is a chemical agent, not an inert gas.

questions.explanation: NAF-S-III is a chemical clean agent developed as a replacement for halon.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAF-S-III replaces halon.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes FM-200 from argon?
questions.explanation: FM-200 is a chemical clean agent (HFC-227ea) with fast discharge. It is widely used in data centers and leaves no residue; argon is an inert gas.
questions.discriminator_tested: FM-200 is chemical; argon is inert.

questions.stem: Two core switches run as one logical switch, and each access switch has an uplink to both. One core switch fails. What is the MOST likely result?

options.rationale: Correct: one failure doesn't cut connectivity.
They keep the uplink to the survivor.

options.text: The network stays up, more slowly
options.rationale: Capacity drops, but continuity is the point.

questions.explanation: Switch clustering makes multiple switches operate as one logical switch, so a single switch failure doesn't cut connectivity.
questions.discriminator_tested: One switch failure doesn't cut connectivity.

questions.stem: Every host on a subnet points to one default gateway address. What BEST keeps that gateway available if its router fails?

options.rationale: Still a single point of failure.

options.text: Two routers with two gateway IPs
options.rationale: Hosts would need reconfiguring on failure.
Reroutes paths, but hosts still point at the dead gateway.
Correct: HSRP or VRRP share a virtual gateway address.

questions.explanation: Router redundancy uses redundant routers and multiple paths with a first-hop redundancy protocol, so the default gateway stays available.
questions.discriminator_tested: The default gateway stays available.

questions.stem: After a firewall pair fails over, every user's VPN and web sessions drop and must reconnect. What was MOST likely missing?

options.rationale: Correct: shared state lets sessions survive failover.
Different rules would block, not reset, sessions.

options.text: A third firewall in the cluster
options.rationale: More units don't carry state over.
Shortens the gap, but sessions still drop.

questions.explanation: Firewall redundancy uses high-availability pairs (active/standby or active/active) that share session state. State sharing lets sessions survive failover.
questions.discriminator_tested: State sharing lets sessions survive failover.

questions.stem: Which two remove single points of failure inside a server? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Server redundancy uses clustering, load balancing, redundant power supplies, and RAID. It removes single points of failure.
questions.discriminator_tested: Removes single points of failure.

questions.stem: When a company compares types of disaster recovery sites, what is the MAIN trade-off?

options.rationale: A backup decision, not a site decision.
A factor, but not the main trade-off.

questions.explanation: Disaster recovery sites are alternate locations to resume operations. The choice is a trade-off between cost and recovery time.
questions.discriminator_tested: Trade-off between cost and recovery time.

questions.stem: A company's recovery agreement is summarized below. What type of recovery site is this?
questions.exhibit:
DR agreement - Plainfield facility
Floor space:   reserved, 400 sq ft
Power / HVAC:  provided
Network:       carrier handoff in place
Equipment:     customer-supplied at time of disaster
Data:          none held on site

options.rationale: Would be fully equipped with replicated data.
Correct: space, power, and connectivity, but no equipment or data.

questions.explanation: A cold site provides space with power and connectivity but no equipment or data. It is the cheapest and slowest option (days to weeks).
questions.discriminator_tested: Cold: cheapest and slowest.

questions.stem: A company can tolerate about two days of downtime and has a moderate budget. Which recovery site BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: middle ground in cost and time.
Meets the target, but costs far more than needed.

questions.explanation: A warm site is partly equipped, with data restored from backups. It is the middle ground in cost and time.
questions.discriminator_tested: Warm: middle ground.

questions.stem: An online brokerage must resume trading within minutes of losing its primary data center, whatever the cost. Which recovery site BEST fits?

options.text: A warm site restored from backup
A cold site with leased space
A hot site with live data replication
A cloud site scaled on demand
options.rationale: Can be fast, but minutes needs a fully running copy.

questions.explanation: A hot site is fully equipped with near-real-time data replication. It is the fastest and most expensive option.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hot: fastest and most expensive.

questions.stem: A company moves its recovery site to a cloud provider. What does its recovery now MOST depend on?

options.rationale: The primary site is the one that failed.

options.text: Spare hardware at a second site
The size of its tape library

questions.explanation: A cloud site is a recovery environment in a cloud provider, scaled on demand. It has lower upfront cost and is elastic, but it depends on connectivity, the provider, and testing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Cloud site depends on connectivity and provider.

questions.stem: A load-balanced web pool is shown below. If node-b fails, what is the MOST likely result?
questions.exhibit:
Pool web-prod  (active/active)
node-a   UP   load 70%
node-b   UP   load 65%

options.rationale: It keeps sending traffic to node-a.
Correct: about 135% of one node's capacity lands on it.

questions.explanation: Active/active vs active/passive: in active/active every node serves traffic; in active/passive a standby takes over on failure. Active/active shares load but loses capacity on failure; active/passive leaves resources idle.
questions.discriminator_tested: Active/active loses capacity on failure.

questions.stem: A company buys internet service from two ISPs. A backhoe cuts one conduit outside the building, and both links go down. What BEST explains this?

options.text: The ISPs share an upstream carrier
options.rationale: Possible, but a cut conduit is a path problem.
No path survived to fail over to.

options.text: Both circuits shared one physical path

questions.explanation: Multiple ISPs and diverse paths mean more than one provider and physically separate routes. Diversity must be physical; two contracts in one conduit still share a failure point.
questions.discriminator_tested: Diversity must be physical.

questions.stem: Which two describe a tabletop exercise? (Choose two.)

options.text: Backups are restored to test servers
Roles and plans are tested by discussion
Systems are failed over to the DR site
Users are phished to test awareness

questions.explanation: Tabletop exercises have a team talk through a disaster scenario without touching systems. They are discussion only and test roles and plans.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tabletop is discussion only.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a validation test from a tabletop exercise?

options.text: It is a discussion of a scenario
It's done after a real disaster

questions.explanation: Validation tests are hands-on tests that confirm recovery procedures and systems work. They actually exercise systems, unlike a tabletop.
questions.discriminator_tested: Validation exercises systems.

questions.stem: Which two belong in a disaster recovery plan rather than the wider business continuity plan? (Choose two.)

options.text: The order for bringing systems back online
Arrangements for staff to work from home
Steps to restore servers from backup

questions.explanation: A disaster recovery plan documents procedures to restore IT systems and data after a disruption. It is IT-focused and part of the broader business continuity plan.
questions.discriminator_tested: DRP is IT-focused restoration.

questions.stem: During a week-long outage, staff take customer orders by phone and on paper forms. Which plan covers this?

options.rationale: Restores IT; doesn't run the business meanwhile.

questions.explanation: A business continuity plan keeps critical business operations running during and after a disruption. It is broader than IT; the DRP is part of it.
questions.discriminator_tested: BCP is broader than IT.

questions.stem: Which two are disaster prevention measures rather than recovery measures? (Choose two.)

options.text: Buying a cyber insurance policy for losses
options.rationale: Risk transfer: it pays for losses but doesn't prevent them.

options.text: Restoring servers at the DR site
Rebuilding a server from its image
Replacing aging disks before they fail
options.rationale: Correct: lowers the likelihood of failure.

options.text: Raised floors in a flood-prone area
options.rationale: Correct: lowers the likelihood of flood damage.

questions.explanation: Disaster prevention and recovery: prevention lowers the likelihood of disruptive events; recovery restores service when they happen.
questions.discriminator_tested: Prevention lowers likelihood; recovery restores service.

questions.stem: A company's "backup" is RAID 5 plus hourly snapshots on the same NAS. The NAS controller fails and corrupts the array. What BEST describes the flaw?

options.rationale: True, but a controller failure isn't a disk failure.

options.text: No separate copy of the data existed
options.rationale: Correct: redundancy and snapshots on one device aren't backups.
They were lost with the array anyway.

options.text: The NAS wasn't on a UPS

questions.explanation: Data loss comes from hardware failure, deletion, corruption, ransomware, or disaster. Backups are the primary defense, and they must be separate from the system they protect.
questions.discriminator_tested: Backups are the primary defense; redundancy isn't a backup.

questions.stem: A user accidentally deletes one folder from a file server. Which backup type restores it with the least time and storage?

options.rationale: Correct: fast and small, and restores individual files.

options.text: A RAID 1 mirror of the disk

options.rationale: Can do it, but it is larger and heavier to work with.

questions.explanation: File-level backups copy selected files and folders. They are fast and small and restore individual files, but can't rebuild a whole system alone.
questions.discriminator_tested: File-level: fast, small, restores individual files.

questions.stem: What BEST describes the main trade-off of image-based backups compared with file-level ones?

options.text: They leave out user data files

options.rationale: File-level backups are better at that.

options.text: They take longer to run each night
options.rationale: Often true, but it's a consequence of the size.

questions.explanation: Image-based backups capture the entire disk or system (OS, applications, settings, data). They enable a full-system (bare-metal) restore but are larger.
questions.discriminator_tested: Image: bare-metal restore; larger.

questions.stem: After a site-wide outage at an online retailer, which restore order BEST follows business criticality?

options.rationale: Correct: revenue first, the blog last.
Order comes from criticality, not speed.
The least critical system goes first.

questions.explanation: Critical applications are those essential to operations. Identifying them sets backup frequency and recovery order; priority comes from business criticality.
questions.discriminator_tested: Priority comes from business criticality.

questions.stem: A router's flash fails, and it is replaced with the same model. What BEST lets the admin restore its routing and ACL setup?

options.text: An image of the admin's laptop

options.rationale: Correct: device backups hold the configuration.
Holds user data, not the router's config.

questions.explanation: Network device backup and restore saves device configurations (for example, copy running-config to a remote server) and restores them after a failure. It backs up configs, not user data.
questions.discriminator_tested: Backs up configs, not user data.

questions.stem: Using the details below, which statement BEST describes this outage?
questions.exhibit:
Nightly full backup:  23:00   (last good: Tue 23:00)
Server failure:       Wed 18:00
Restore duration:     about 2 hours

options.text: No data lost, since a backup exists
options.rationale: Changes after the backup are lost.

options.text: Data since the last backup is lost
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't quantify loss or restore time.
Correct: data loss runs back to the last backup.

questions.explanation: Data restoration characteristics describe how fast and how current a restore is. RTO is the time to restore; RPO is the tolerable data loss, set by the age of the last backup.
questions.discriminator_tested: RPO is set by the age of the last backup.

questions.stem: A company's sole backup is a USB drive left permanently plugged into the file server. What is the MAIN risk?

options.text: Ransomware or fire takes both copies
options.rationale: Correct: it is online and onsite.

options.text: USB drives hold too little data
The USB drive may wear out
options.rationale: Possible, but the bigger risk is shared fate.

questions.explanation: Backup media (disk or NAS, tape, cloud, removable media) trade off cost, speed, capacity, and durability. Offline or offsite media survive ransomware and site loss; an always-attached drive does neither.
questions.discriminator_tested: Offline or offsite media survive ransomware and site loss.

questions.stem: Weeknight backups must be quick, yet a restore may need no more than two backup sets. Which scheme BEST fits?

options.text: A monthly full and nothing else
options.rationale: Loses up to a month of data.
One set to restore, but slow every night.
Restore needs the full plus every incremental.
Correct: restore needs the full plus the latest differential.

questions.explanation: Backup methods: full (everything), incremental (changes since the last backup of any type), differential (changes since the last full). A differential restore needs the full plus the latest differential.
questions.discriminator_tested: Differential restore: full plus latest differential.

questions.stem: Which two things does a periodic test restore verify? (Choose two.)

options.text: The backup job logged a success status
options.rationale: A log says nothing about restorability.

options.text: The restore fits within the RTO
The data is complete and intact

questions.explanation: Backup testing means periodically restoring data to verify integrity, completeness, and timing. An untested backup is unproven.
questions.discriminator_tested: Test restores verify integrity, completeness, timing.

questions.stem: A service restores online account access for anyone who answers the account's security questions. What is the MAIN risk?

options.text: Resets take too long to process

options.rationale: Correct: birthplaces and pet names are often public.
An inconvenience, not the security risk.

questions.explanation: Online account recovery resets access through email, phone, recovery codes, or MFA. The recovery channel is itself an attack path; protect it.
questions.discriminator_tested: The recovery channel is an attack path.

questions.stem: A standalone laptop has one local admin account and no recovery media. The admin password is lost. What is the MAIN problem?

options.text: Disk encryption may block offline tools
options.rationale: Only if it's encrypted; not stated.

options.text: The domain help desk is slow
options.rationale: The laptop isn't in a domain.

options.text: The account unlocks after an hour
options.rationale: Lockout timers don't fix a lost password.

options.text: No second admin or central reset
options.rationale: Correct: local recovery depends on one of those or physical tools.

questions.explanation: Local account recovery is a reset by another local administrator or with recovery media or tools. It depends on a second admin account or physical access; there is no central reset.
questions.discriminator_tested: Local recovery: no central reset.

questions.stem: A domain user is locked out at 2 a.m., and the help desk is closed until 8. What BEST lets the user recover now?

options.rationale: The lockout is held in the directory.

options.text: Waiting for the help desk to open
A local admin on the PC

questions.explanation: Domain account recovery is a reset or unlock by a domain administrator or help desk in the directory. It is managed centrally, and self-service reset is possible.
questions.discriminator_tested: Self-service reset is possible.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a battery backup from a generator?
questions.explanation: A battery backup provides short-term power during an outage. Its runtime is in minutes, not hours; a generator runs for hours but needs time to start.
questions.discriminator_tested: Battery: minutes, not hours.

questions.stem: Which two does a UPS provide? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: A UPS is battery-backed power that also conditions input power. It bridges to a graceful shutdown or generator start; it isn't long-term power.
questions.discriminator_tested: UPS: battery power plus conditioning; not long-term.

questions.stem: A home office wants the cheapest UPS for one desktop PC and can accept a brief switchover gap. Which BEST fits?
questions.explanation: A standby UPS passes utility power and switches to battery on failure. It has a brief switchover gap and offers the lowest cost and least protection.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standby: lowest cost, brief gap.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a line-interactive UPS from a standby UPS?

options.text: It usually costs a bit more
It evens out sags without the battery
It is started by a generator
options.rationale: A UPS bridges to a generator.

questions.explanation: A line-interactive UPS regulates voltage sags and surges without using the battery, then switches to battery on an outage. It handles voltage fluctuation at mid-range cost.
questions.discriminator_tested: Line-interactive handles voltage fluctuation.

questions.stem: What is the MAIN trade-off of an online (double-conversion) UPS?

options.text: A brief gap when it switches
It runs warmer and uses more power

options.rationale: Correct: no transfer time, highest price.

questions.explanation: An online UPS uses double conversion: equipment always runs from the inverter. There is no transfer time, giving the best protection at the highest cost.
questions.discriminator_tested: Online: best protection, highest cost.

questions.stem: During an outage, a diesel generator fails to start because its fuel had degraded over two years. What was MOST clearly missing?

options.text: A UPS with a larger battery

options.rationale: Its fuel would have aged too.
Correct: generators need fuel and testing.

questions.explanation: Power generators provide long-duration backup power (diesel or natural gas). They take time to start, so a UPS bridges the gap, and they need fuel and testing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Generators need fuel and testing.

questions.stem: An office plugs its server into a surge protector and believes it's now covered for outages. What BEST describes the problem?

options.rationale: True, but the outage is the gap here.

options.text: It needs a PDU behind it
options.rationale: A PDU adds no backup either.

options.text: It should be a rack-mount model
It has no battery to run on
options.rationale: Correct: it protects against spikes, not outages.

questions.explanation: Surge protection diverts excess voltage spikes away from equipment. It protects against spikes, not outages, and isn't a UPS.
questions.discriminator_tested: Spikes, not outages.

questions.stem: A rack's power path is shown below. What BEST lets the rack ride through a short utility outage?
questions.exhibit:
Rack R4 power path
Utility feed A --> Switched PDU (24 outlets) --> 6 servers
Utility feed A --> Metered PDU  (24 outlets) --> 2 switches

options.rationale: Helps with long outages, but leaves a gap while it starts.
Correct: a PDU gains backup only when fed by a UPS.

questions.explanation: A PDU distributes power to rack equipment; metered and switched versions add monitoring and remote outlet control. It is distribution, not backup, and gains backup only when fed by a UPS.
questions.discriminator_tested: PDU gains backup only when fed by a UPS.

questions.stem: A server room's HVAC is sized for today's load, but 20 more servers are being installed next month. What is the MAIN risk?

options.rationale: Heat load rarely sets it off.
Likely, but not the continuity risk.
Correct: more heat than the cooling can remove.
Not the main effect of extra load.

questions.explanation: HVAC controls temperature, airflow, and humidity. Overheating causes failures, so cooling capacity is a continuity control.
questions.discriminator_tested: Overheating causes failures.

questions.stem: A server room's relative humidity climbs to 85% for several days. What is the MOST likely consequence?

options.rationale: Humidity, not temperature, is out of range.
Possible, but not the main hazard.
That comes from air that is too dry.

questions.explanation: ASHRAE standards recommend temperature and humidity ranges for computing environments (about 18-27 C). Air that is too humid causes condensation and corrosion; too dry raises static risk.
questions.discriminator_tested: Too humid = condensation and corrosion.

questions.stem: What should MOST guide the choice of a fire suppression system?

options.rationale: Safety matters, but the contents drive the choice.
Correct: match the system to the space.

questions.explanation: Fire suppression extinguishes fires while limiting damage to people and equipment. Match the system to the space: water-based versus clean agent.
questions.discriminator_tested: Match the system to the space.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a wet pipe system from a dry pipe system?

options.text: Water is held in the pipes constantly

questions.explanation: Wet pipe systems keep water in the pipes; heat opens a sprinkler head. They are the simplest and fastest, but accidental discharge or leaks can damage electronics.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wet pipe: water always in the pipes.

questions.stem: What is the MAIN drawback of a dry pipe system compared with a wet pipe system?

options.rationale: Freezing areas are where it's used.
Correct: gas must escape before water arrives.
That is a wet pipe concern.

questions.explanation: Dry pipe systems hold pressurized gas; water enters after a head opens. They are used where pipes could freeze, at the cost of slower water delivery.
questions.discriminator_tested: Dry pipe: slower water delivery.

questions.stem: A data center wants water-based suppression with the lowest chance of accidental discharge. Which BEST fits?

options.rationale: One trigger: a head opening admits water.
Correct: detection plus an opened head.

questions.explanation: Preaction systems keep the pipes dry; water enters after detection, and a head must then open. The two-step trigger lowers accidental-discharge risk, which makes them common in data centers.
questions.discriminator_tested: Two-step trigger lowers accidental-discharge risk.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a deluge system from a preaction system?

options.text: Heads open one at a time

questions.explanation: Deluge systems have open heads that discharge water from every head on detection. They deliver massive water flow for high-hazard areas.
questions.discriminator_tested: Deluge: open heads, massive flow.

questions.stem: A small enclosed room holds a company's core servers and its tape library. Which suppression system BEST fits?

options.rationale: Lowers accidental discharge, but still wets equipment when it fires.
Correct: no water damage, no residue.

questions.explanation: Clean agent systems use gaseous suppression that leaves no residue. There is no water damage, so they suit equipment rooms.
questions.discriminator_tested: Clean agent suits equipment rooms.

questions.stem: An old data center still has a working halon system. What BEST describes its status?

options.rationale: True, but it doesn't describe its status.

options.text: Legacy; no new halon is produced
options.rationale: Correct: production is banned for ozone damage.

questions.explanation: Halon is an effective gaseous agent that depletes ozone. Its production is banned (EPA); legacy systems are what remain.
questions.discriminator_tested: Halon production banned; legacy only.

questions.stem: An argon system protects a control room where operators work. What is the MAIN safety concern?

options.rationale: Correct: it works by oxygen reduction.

questions.explanation: Argon is an inert gas that displaces oxygen. It is safe for equipment and works by oxygen reduction, so people must evacuate before discharge.
questions.discriminator_tested: Argon works by oxygen reduction.

questions.stem: Which two are chemical clean agents used as halon replacements? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: NAF-S-III is a chemical clean agent developed as a halon replacement. FM-200 (HFC-227ea) is another, widely used in data centers; argon is an inert gas.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAF-S-III and FM-200 are chemical halon replacements.

questions.stem: A data center wants a fast-discharging chemical clean agent, widely used in equipment rooms, that leaves no residue. Which BEST fits?
questions.explanation: FM-200 is a chemical clean agent (HFC-227ea) with fast discharge. It is widely used in data centers and leaves no residue.
questions.discriminator_tested: FM-200: chemical, fast, no residue.

questions.stem: A company wants its network core to survive a switch failure without spanning-tree reconvergence, managed as one device. Which BEST fits?

options.rationale: Redundant, but reconverges and is managed separately.

questions.explanation: Switch clustering makes multiple switches operate as one logical switch. A single switch failure doesn't cut connectivity.
questions.discriminator_tested: One logical switch; one failure doesn't cut connectivity.

questions.stem: Hosts use 10.1.1.1 as their default gateway. Given the output below, what is the MOST likely result if R1 fails?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show standby brief
Interface  Grp  Pri  State   Active  Standby   Virtual IP
Gi0/1      10   110  Active  local   10.1.1.3  10.1.1.1

options.rationale: The virtual IP moves; hosts don't change.
True during failover, but not the key outcome.
Correct: the standby assumes the virtual gateway.

questions.explanation: Router redundancy uses redundant routers and multiple paths with a first-hop redundancy protocol such as HSRP. The default gateway stays available.
questions.discriminator_tested: The default gateway stays available.

questions.stem: Which two make a firewall pair's failover transparent to users? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keeping a third unit powered off

options.rationale: Correct: the standby enforces the same rules.

questions.explanation: Firewall redundancy uses high-availability pairs (active/standby or active/active) that share session state. State sharing lets sessions survive failover.
questions.discriminator_tested: State sharing lets sessions survive failover.

questions.stem: A web app runs on one server with RAID 1 and dual power supplies. The motherboard fails, and the app goes down. What BEST describes what was missing?

options.rationale: Speeds the repair, but the app still goes down.

questions.explanation: Server redundancy uses clustering, load balancing, redundant power supplies, and RAID to remove single points of failure. The server itself was still one.
questions.discriminator_tested: Removes single points of failure.

questions.stem: A CFO asks for the fastest possible disaster recovery at the lowest possible price. What BEST describes the planner's answer?

options.text: Site types recover at similar speeds
options.rationale: They range from minutes to weeks.
True, but they still trade cost against speed.
True, but not the trade-off asked about.

questions.explanation: Disaster recovery sites are alternate locations to resume operations. The choice is a trade-off between cost and recovery time.
questions.discriminator_tested: Trade-off between cost and recovery time.

questions.stem: A company's disaster recovery plan relies on a cold site. What is the MAIN drawback?

options.text: Equipment must be bought or shipped
options.rationale: True; it's the reason for the delay.

options.text: Data is replicated in real time
options.rationale: A cold site holds no data.

questions.explanation: A cold site provides space with power and connectivity but no equipment or data. It is the cheapest and slowest option (days to weeks).
questions.discriminator_tested: Cold: cheapest and slowest.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a warm site from a hot site?

options.text: It runs in a cloud provider
It generally costs less to run
options.rationale: True, but a result of the difference.
Correct: partly equipped, data from backups.

questions.explanation: A warm site is partly equipped, with data restored from backups: the middle ground in cost and time. A hot site has near-real-time replication.
questions.discriminator_tested: Warm: data restored from backups.

questions.stem: A company pays for a fully equipped hot site but replicates data to it once a week. What BEST describes the problem?

options.text: Data at the site can be a week old
options.rationale: Correct: hot sites rely on near-real-time replication.

options.text: It wastes the hot site's cost
options.rationale: A consequence of the stale data.
Replication is what makes them hot.

questions.explanation: A hot site is fully equipped with near-real-time data replication. It is the fastest and most expensive option, and weekly replication defeats its purpose.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hot site needs near-real-time replication.

questions.stem: A startup with little capital needs a recovery environment that can scale up on demand. Which BEST fits?

options.rationale: Slow, and doesn't scale on demand.

questions.explanation: A cloud site is a recovery environment in a cloud provider, scaled on demand. It has lower upfront cost and is elastic, but depends on connectivity, the provider, and testing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Cloud: lower upfront cost, elastic.

questions.stem: A team wants no loss of capacity when one node fails and accepts that the second node sits idle until then. Which design BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: the standby takes over at full capacity.
Shares load, but loses capacity on failure.
Can work, but the team chose idle standby.

questions.explanation: Active/active vs active/passive: in active/active every node serves traffic; in active/passive a standby takes over on failure. Active/active shares load but loses capacity on failure; active/passive leaves resources idle.
questions.discriminator_tested: Active/passive leaves resources idle.

questions.stem: Which two give a site real internet path diversity? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Same provider, possibly the same path.

questions.explanation: Multiple ISPs and diverse paths mean more than one provider and physically separate routes. Diversity must be physical; two contracts in one conduit still share a failure point.
questions.discriminator_tested: Diversity must be physical.

questions.stem: A team wants to check whether staff know their roles in the recovery plan, with no risk to production systems. Which exercise is BEST?

options.rationale: Hands-on; tests systems more than roles.

questions.explanation: Tabletop exercises have a team talk through a disaster scenario without touching systems. They are discussion only and test roles and plans.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tabletop: discussion only; tests roles and plans.

questions.stem: A company's recovery plan has been talked through in tabletop exercises every year, but never run on real systems. What is MOST clearly missing?

options.rationale: Correct: confirms procedures and systems work.

questions.explanation: Validation tests are hands-on tests that confirm recovery procedures and systems work. They actually exercise systems, unlike a tabletop.
questions.discriminator_tested: Validation actually exercises systems.

questions.stem: What BEST describes the focus of a disaster recovery plan?
questions.explanation: A disaster recovery plan documents procedures to restore IT systems and data after a disruption. It is IT-focused restoration.
questions.discriminator_tested: DRP is IT-focused.

questions.stem: How does a business continuity plan relate to a disaster recovery plan?

options.text: The DRP is one part of the BCP
The BCP is one part of the DRP

questions.explanation: A business continuity plan keeps critical business operations running during and after a disruption. It is broader than IT; the DRP is part of it.
questions.discriminator_tested: BCP is broader; DRP is part of it.
